title: How to Clean a Cast Iron Skillet Without Ruining the Seasoning
description: Learn how to clean a cast iron skillet safely using warm water, kosher salt, and zero soap damage. Master proper maintenance for lasting non-stick pans.
story: There is a stubborn myth that washing cast iron with soap and water is an unpardonable kitchen sin. For years, I wiped my favorite #8 Wagner skillet down with just a dry paper towel after frying bacon, convincing myself that residual grease counted as seasoning. It didn't. It just went rancid and sticky by Tuesday morning. Modern dish soap will not strip a well-polymerized layer of oil, but ignoring stuck-on scrambled eggs definitely invites rust. When testing this method, I learned the hard way that letting a pan soak for even five minutes in the sink creates flash rust along the rim before you even grab the dish towel. Now, I tackle baked-on dinner messes while the iron is still warm to the touch, using coarse salt as a gentle abrasive that respects the patina built over decades of Sunday morning pancakes.
ingredients: 1 heavy-duty cast iron skillet with stuck-on food
A stiff-bristled nylon brush or chainmail scrubber
1 tsp neutral canola or grapeseed oil
Clean cotton kitchen towels or paper towels
instructions: Run warm tap water over the warm skillet, being careful not to thermal-shock a freezing pan with scalding water.
Pour coarse kosher salt directly into the center of the wet pan to create a natural, non-scratch scouring paste.
Scrub the surface firmly in circular motions using a stiff nylon brush or chainmail pad, focusing on burnt edges without pressing so hard you gouge the iron.
Rinse the skillet thoroughly with warm water, washing away all loosened food debris and grey salt slurry down the drain.
Place the washed skillet directly on a burner over medium-low heat for 2 to 3 minutes until every last drop of moisture evaporates.
Turn off the burner, apply a mere half-teaspoon of neutral oil, and buff it entirely across the cooking surface and outer walls with a dry paper towel until the pan looks satin-matte, not slick.
proHack: If your skillet develops a sticky, uneven texture, bake it upside down in your oven at 450°F for an hour with a micro-thin layer of Crisco to reset the polymerized base.
servingIdea: Keep your restored skillet right on the stovetop burner so it is warm, dry, and instantly ready for your next batch of weeknight cornbread or seared ribeyes.
storage: Store your clean skillet in a dry kitchen cabinet with a folded paper towel tucked between the rim and lid to allow air circulation and prevent moisture trapping.

faqs.question: Can I actually use dish soap on cast iron?
faqs.answer: Yes, modern dish soap contains very mild surfactants that will not harm seasoned cast iron. However, avoid harsh commercial scouring powders and never put the pan in the automatic dishwasher.

faqs.question: What should I do if my skillet turns orange with rust?
faqs.answer: Do not panic. Scour the rust spots completely away using steel wool and warm soapy water, dry the pan thoroughly on the stove, and apply a fresh coat of oil to re-season it.
